slides.0.title: Geography and climate
slides.0.subtitle: Mediterranean climate, winds, soils and two sub-regions
slides.1.title: Extent and scale
slides.1.highlights.0.title: One of the world's largest
slides.1.highlights.0.content: Wine With Seth calls it the world's largest wine region with a geographic identity, producing over a third of French wine; its area figures conflict (700,000 acres vs 230,000 ha), so we do not use them
slides.1.highlights.1.title: Two parts
slides.1.highlights.1.content: Languedoc is about 90% of combined output and Roussillon about 10% (Wine With Seth)
slides.1.highlights.2.title: A naming trap
slides.1.highlights.2.content: "Languedoc" can mean the historic region or the northern part of today's region; Roussillon is in the Pyrénées-Orientales, while Aude and Hérault belong to Languedoc
slides.1.content: Get the geography straight first and appellation names stop being confusing.
slides.2.title: A Mediterranean climate
slides.2.highlights.0.title: Sunshine
slides.2.highlights.0.content: Over 2,500 hours a year (Wine With Seth)
slides.2.highlights.1.title: Dry summers, wet winters
slides.2.highlights.1.content: May to August is very dry and most rain falls in winter; drought is the most common threat (Wikipedia)
slides.2.highlights.2.title: Extreme weather
slides.2.highlights.2.content: Wikipedia cites 1999, when a year's rain fell in 36 hours over Corbières and Minervois, and May hail in Roussillon
slides.2.content: Plenty of light and heat but scarce water is the starting point for understanding the region.
slides.3.title: Winds and altitude
slides.3.highlights.0.title: Tramontane
slides.3.highlights.0.content: A dry northwesterly funnelled between the Pyrenees and Massif Central; it suppresses disease and supports organic viticulture (Wine With Seth)
slides.3.highlights.1.title: Marin
slides.3.highlights.1.content: A warm, moist southeasterly sea wind, mainly in spring and autumn (Wine With Seth)
slides.3.highlights.2.title: Terrain
slides.3.highlights.2.content: Languedoc lies mainly on coastal plains and river valleys; Roussillon sits in narrow valleys and terraces around the Pyrenees at higher elevation; the Massif Central and Cévennes bound the north
slides.3.content: Wind is the key natural crop protection, while mountains and sea create varied mesoclimates.
slides.4.title: Soil diversity
slides.4.highlights.0.title: Limestone and alluvial
slides.4.highlights.0.content: Inland: chalk, limestone and gravel; near the coast, more alluvial soils (Wikipedia); La Clape is largely limestone
slides.4.highlights.1.title: Schist and granite
slides.4.highlights.1.content: Faugères and parts of Saint-Chinian are on schist; granite and clay also occur
slides.4.highlights.2.title: Ancient river stones
slides.4.highlights.2.content: Some highly rated vineyards sit on ancient riverbed stones similar to Châteauneuf-du-Pape's (Wikipedia)
slides.4.content: Soil diversity is the thread for studying the appellations one by one in Level 2.
